about: The Country and the city's loop (Docs/Design/68-the-country-and-the-city-loop.md). The Country stands for the farms, mines, woods and villages beyond the walls until they are built: what a keeper draws from the store room is bought from it (its purse is the account outside:<market id>), and every day it spends what it took in on the city's goods, keeping a reserve. `markets` is a list so that the smaller towns can each become a market with its own purse and basket later; there is one for now. A market's `basket` is what its people buy in the city, as shares of its day's spending (any whole numbers; they are scaled to the money it has), weighted toward the trades with time to spare (tools/city_loop.py checks it against the city's makers). `wages` says who pays a post that is neither a shop's keeper nor its hand (those are paid by their shop's till) nor the watch (the treasury): the first rule with a word in the post's title, in lower case. `food` and `comforts` are the residents' buying. The numbers are placeholders; the per-world settings (on and off, the reserve, the toll, the wages, carriage, goods the Country no longer supplies) are the world's own, in live.economy and Atlas's Economy page.

markets.name: the Country
markets.people: the country folk not yet placed (Docs/Design/66-worlds-atlas-and-dm.md, 2): when they are given farms, their farms take over the goods they grow

rules.about: The heads of the Crown's household and of the city's offices (doc 68, Progress, "First fixes"): the Queen, the King's daughter, the City Office's head; and ("Trades": the user, 2026-10-31, office heads get a head's pay) the King, the two chancellors, the royal secretary, the Crown's treasurer, the magistrate, the keeper of the rolls (the Records Office), the collector of customs, the warden of the Market Hall, the abbot, the keepers of the Washhouse and the Bathhouse, and the Watch's commander (a guard: the watch's post, at this wage). Paid by the treasury at a keeper's wage (a head's), not a clerk's.

The Minor Houses' family members who run a House's own affairs (doc 68, Progress, "First fixes"): a House's lending, the Grayrock wharf; and the heads of the Houses' offices ("Trades"): the harbourmaster of the Wharf Office, the Counting House's overseer. Kept by their House's estates in the Country (as the Houses' other people), at a keeper's wage.
Carriage by sea and the Country's warehouses: the ships' unloading, the cranes, the carrying up from the wharf, the stores' tallies.
The Great and Minor Houses' people, kept by their estates in the Country: heads, stewards, servants, the Houses' own trades.

Public posts: the Crown and the Council, the courts, the offices, the Records Office, the customs, the lamps, the markets' hands, the washhouse and baths, the teachers, the abbey, the cathedral and the chapels.

food.about: Each household goes to market once a day at its own hour, and tops every member up to `days` days of food; one still short of `shortDays` tries again each hour until the shops shut. Food is picked among what the open shops have, the better the nourishment for the price the likelier. Whoever in the household has the money pays.

comforts.about: A household holding more than `above` pennies a head spends `share` of what is over it a day on comforts from the city's shops, used up at once: the better-off buy drink, candles, cloth and treats, so that savings come back to the shops. (Doc 68, Progress, "First fixes": 40p and a fifth, as set 2 measured; at most `rules.comfortsMost` purchases a day.) The day's budget pays for the city's services first (`services`), then comforts.

rules.about: The loop's rules the DM can tune (Docs/Design/68-the-country-and-the-city-loop.md, Progress, "First fixes"; each world's own in live.economy.rules, migration 0058, the DM's Economy tab and Atlas's Economy page). comfortsMost: the most comforts a household buys a day (it was 20, which kept the rich from spending their savings). almsADay: pennies a head the city's alms make a household up to after the day's wages (was 7: a day's food with nothing over for a Restday). treasuryCap: pennies the treasury keeps; what it holds over this at 18:00, after its own posts, pays what the shops' tills could not pay their posts (wageSupport percent of each till's shortfall; each post the same share of its wage). workBankHours: the crew's hours a shop may bank for a long craft, in hours of the whole crew's work; 0 (the default): as long as the business's longest craft and an hour more (at least two), so a lone cartographer can make a map over two days (was 2, which no 13.9-hour map could fit). fairFood: 1 = at market the members with least food buy first, everyone to `food.shortDays` before anyone to `food.days`, and only foods some member can pay for are picked; 0 = the old order. services: 1 = households buy the city's services (`services`) from their comforts budget; 0 = none. servicesCityShare: the percent of each service's price that goes to the treasury (the city); the rest stays in the shop's till. Trades and the follow-ups (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"): suppliers: 1 = a keeper buys its craft inputs from the city's makers first (`suppliers`: the cooper's casks for the wine makers), at their price, till to till; 0 = all from the store room. patrons: 1 = the trades' patrons (`patrons`: the treasury, the Houses' estates, the wharf) pay for their units' work (the services `for: patrons`) and the armoury's new kit; 0 = none. armourEvery: days between new pieces of kit for each armed wolf. buyAheadDays: days of food more a household buys the day before a Restday or festival (0: none). floatDrawDays: a till's working float, kept back before its wages and its keeper's profit, is its mean draws a day over this many days (1: yesterday's, as it was). floatWagesDays: days of its posts' wages a till keeps over its float before profit (7, a week, as it was). subsidyToNeed: 1 = the carriage subsidy gives the carters only what their till lacks of tonight's wages and its float (nothing to their keeper's profit); 0 = a quarter of all carriage, as it was.

services.about: The city's services (the user, 2026-10-31: "Make them public services that NPC's have the occasional need to purchase from, but make it items that NPC's buy when they have excess money that isn't needed for other things. The money goes partly to the shop owner and to the city."). Each is a catalogue item (category service, items.json: its name and its price) a business does for a household: bought only from the household's comforts budget (what is over `comforts.above` a head, after food, needs and their reserve), at its market hour, about once every `every` days (a fixed roll of the household and the day: nothing saved), from an open shop of `business` in its community (else anywhere open). Done at once: nothing is kept on a shelf or at home. Of its price `rules.servicesCityShare` percent goes to the treasury, the rest to the shop's till. Each world may turn one off or change its price and frequency (live.economy.services). A service `for: patrons` (doc 68, Progress, "Trades") is never a household's: it is done for each unit of its business's patrons (`patrons`: an armed wolf, a hull, a building) about once every `every` days, paid by the patron, with no city share.

suppliers.about: The city's makers that supply another business's craft inputs first (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"; the rule suppliers): what a `buyer`'s keeper draws for its crafts it buys from a `seller`'s till holding it, at the seller's price (the catalogue's, a dearer season's after), till to till inside the walls (no toll, no carriage), and from the store room only what the city's sellers lack. `goods`: the goods it covers (none: every input the seller sells). Only craft inputs: a good bought to sell on stays the store room's (bought at a shop's price it would leave the reseller nothing). The wine makers' casks from the cooper for now (wine by the cask: crafts.json); later chains, such as the mill's flour for the bakers, are a line here.

patrons.about: The trades whose customers are the city, the Houses and the wharf rather than households (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"; the user, 2026-10-31, on the armoury: "Armory should have houses and city as customers ... high cost items replaced occasionally, but repaired frequently which should be the main source of their business"; and the follow-ups: the shipwright's hulls for the wharf and sea carriage, the builders' yard's upkeep of the public buildings and the Houses' halls). Each group is a patron with its units: the posts of `roles` (the watch: every guard's post), else `units` (not placed: a number); `payer` the treasury or a market's id (the Houses' estates and the wharf are the Country, as with the Houses' wages). Once a day, at the first hour one of the trade's shops is open, each unit has each of the trade's services `for: patrons` done about once every `every` days (their prices and frequencies: `services`, the DM's), and where the trade has `pieces`, a new piece bought about once every rules.armourEvery days (one of these the shop holds, at the catalogue's price). A payer spends only what it can spare: the treasury over its float and tonight's posts, the Country over its reserve and its posts.

groups.name: the Houses' armed retainers (their estates: none placed yet, a number)
the wharf's and sea carriage's hulls (the Country)
the Houses' halls (their estates, the Country)

shelves.about: Dear goods a shop keeps fewer of on its shelves than the usual four (doc 68, Progress, "Trades"): theriac, the apothecary's rare cure-all, one at a time.

seasons.about: The seasons in the Country's supply (Docs/Design/68-the-country-and-the-city-loop.md, Progress, "Seasons and the DM's rules"): each group's goods, and for Spring, Summer, Autumn and Winter (the value at each season's middle day; the days between blend in a straight line), in percent of normal: `supply`, how much the Country can send the city a day, of `normal` pieces a day for the whole group (0 pieces: no cap; a supply of 0 sends none); `price`, what the group's goods cost, both the shops' draws from the store room and the shops' prices to residents (the residents weigh nourishment for the price, so they buy what is in season); `shelf`, how full the shops keep their shelves of the group's goods (a maker stocking up ahead of a lean season). Goods made of a group's goods sit in it when their price should follow it (bread with the grain). The numbers are placeholders, each world's to change in the DM (its Economy tab) or Atlas's Economy page; `normal` is about what the city drew a day without a cap (build 48).

groups.name: grain and flour
groups.about: Harvested late summer into autumn: plentiful and cheap then, so more bread; dearer and short in winter and spring until the next harvest.

groups.name: fresh fruit
groups.about: Apples, berries and grapes: plentiful from high summer to the autumn's end, scarce in winter.

groups.name: vegetables
groups.about: Fresh from the fields from summer into autumn; little in winter.

groups.name: fresh fish
groups.about: More fresh fish in winter (the user's call, 2026-10-31): the cold months' catch.

groups.name: livestock and meat
groups.about: Kept the year round: no season.

groups.name: milk and dairy
groups.about: The year round, a little less (and dearer) in winter.

groups.name: honey
groups.about: Taken from summer into autumn; scarcer in winter and spring.

groups.name: dried and preserved fruit
groups.about: The preserver's goods keep for months and don't follow the season themselves: their makers stock up in autumn, while fruit is cheap and plentiful (their shelves run to 2.5 times their sales), so there is more of them through the winter, when fresh fruit is scarce (their shelves fall back to normal by spring, so the stock is sold down before more is made). Since doc 68's follow-ups ("winter preserves"): the Country's own stores (`stores`) send them when fresh fruit runs short, a preserver that can't make them for the fruit's cap drawing them itself (at most `normal` pieces a day times `supply`: most in winter, little in summer), and they are a tenth cheaper in winter, so residents eat more of them then, beside the winter's fresh fish.
